en: The Thirteen-Book Collection of Birth Stories (Jātaka),
Chapter on Mangoes (Ambavagga)
4. The Cūḷanāradajātaka:
“The firewood has not been split by you, nor has water been brought by you;”
“Even the fires have not been neglected by you;
why then do you meditate like one who is dull-witted?
“I am unable to dwell in the forest.”
I entreat you, Kassapa:
dwelling in the forest is suffering;
I wish to go to the kingdom.
Just as I, having gone from here to whatever country I dwell in,
would train in the proper conduct, O Brahmā.
“Instruct me in that Dhamma.
“If, having abandoned the forest and its roots and fruits...”
You take delight in dwelling in the kingdom;
listen to this Dhamma from me:
do not consume poison.
Avoid falling into pits;
do not sink into the mud, and proceed with caution where there are venomous snakes.
“What indeed is the poison, the precipice,
or the mire for those who lead the holy life?
Whom do you call a venomous serpent?”
"Tell me that when you are asked:
'Dear one, in this world, what is called "intoxicant" (āsava) is indeed spoken of as "liquor" (surā)."
Pleasant, fragrant, charming,
and sweet like a small amount of soup—
this the Noble Ones call poison.
“Of the holy life, Nārada,
women, dear one, overcome him who is heedless in this world.”
They carry away the mind of the young man like the wind carries a loose tuft of cotton;
this is declared to be a precipice.
O Nārada, gain, fame, honor, and veneration from other families are not the fruit of the holy life.
And this, O Nārada, is declared to be the mire of the holy life (brahmacariya):
kings together with their weapons, my dear.
They dwell upon this earth,
O dear Nārada, under such great human lords.
One should not walk at the feet of lords or masters;
he is declared to be like a venomous serpent.
O Nārada, regarding the holy life:
when one has finished eating at the time for food,
whatever house one may enter;
Whatever wholesome thing one should know to exist here,
therein one should go for alms;
having entered another’s family, [one should act with mindfulness].
For the sake of sustenance or food,
one should eat and consume in moderation,
and not set one's mind on the appearance.
Avoid from afar the drinking hall, liquor,
and gambling, as well as social clubs and scattering of wealth.
"Like those who go astray on a rugged path.
Thus ends the fourth Jātaka, the Cūḷanāradajātaka.
